### What is a Sequential Sampling Plan? {#sec-pmc-26}

[**Sequential Sampling**]{#sec-pmc-26-overview}

Sequential sampling is different from single, double or multiple sampling. Here one takes a sequence of samples from a lot. How many total samples looked at is a function of the results of the sampling process.

[**Item-by-item and group sequential sampling**]{#sec-pmc-26-item-group}

The sequence can be one sample at a time, and then the sampling process is usually called *item-by-item* sequential sampling. One can also select sample sizes greater than one, in which case the process is referred to as *group* sequential sampling. Item-by-item is more popular so we concentrate on it. The operation of such a plan is illustrated below:

[**Diagram of item-by-item sampling**]{#sec-pmc-26-diagram}

![Diagram demonstrating item-by-item sequential sampling plan](test-acceptability/images/sequential-sampling-plan.svg){#fig-pmc-26-seq-plan}

[**Description of sequentail sampling graph**]{#sec-pmc-26-description}

The cumulative observed number of defectives is plotted on the graph. For each point, the x-axis is the total number of items thus far selected, and the y-axis is the total number of observed defectives. If the plotted point falls within the parallel lines the process continues by drawing another sample. As soon as a point falls on or above the upper line, the lot is rejected. And when a point falls on or below the lower line, the lot is accepted. The process can theoretically last until the lot is 100% inspected. However, as a rule of thumb, sequential-sampling plans are truncated after the number inspected reaches three times the number that would have been inspected using a corresponding single sampling plan.

[**Equations for the limit lines**]{#sec-pmc-26-equations}

The equations for the two limit lines are functions of the parameters $p_1$, $\alpha$, $p_2$, and $\beta$.

$$ \begin{aligned}
x_a & = -h_1 + s n \\
x_r & =  h_2 + s n \, ,
\end{aligned} $$

where

$$ \begin{aligned}
  k & = \log  \left[ \frac{p_2(1-p_1)}{p_1(1-p_2)}\right] \\
h_1 & = \frac{1}{k} \left[ \log \left(\frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}\right)  \right] \\
h_2 & = \frac{1}{k} \left[ \log \left(\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}\right)  \right] \\
  s & = \frac{1}{k} \left[ \log \left(\frac{1-p_1}{1-p_2}\right)  \right] \, .
\end{aligned} $$

Instead of using the graph to determine the fate of the lot, one can resort to generating tables (with the help of a computer program).

[**Example of a sequential sampling plan**]{#sec-pmc-26-example}

As an example, let $p_1 = 0.01$, $p_2 = 0.10$, $\alpha = 0.05$, and $\beta = 0.10$. The resulting equations are:

$$ \begin{aligned}
x_a & = -0.939 + 0.04 n \\
x_r & = 1.205 + 0.04 n \, .
\end{aligned} $$

Both acceptance numbers and rejection numbers must be integers. The acceptance number is the next integer less than or equal to $x_a$ and the rejection number is the next integer greater than or equal to $x_r$. Thus for $n=1$, the acceptance number is -1, which is impossible, and the rejection number is 2, which is also impossible. For $n = 24$, the acceptance number is 0 and the rejection number is 3.

The results for $n = 1, \, 2, \, 3, \, \ldots, \, 26$ are tabulated below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pmc-26-seq-table
#| tbl-cap: "Acceptance and rejection numbers for n = 1, ..., 26"
#| code-fold: true
seq_table <- tibble(n = 1:26) |>
  mutate(
    xa = -0.939 + 0.04 * n,
    xr = 1.205 + 0.04 * n,
    accept = floor(xa),
    reject = ceiling(xr),
    accept = ifelse(accept < 0, "x", as.character(accept))
  ) |>
  select(n, accept, reject)

left <- seq_table |> filter(n <= 13) |> rename(n_l = n, accept_l = accept, reject_l = reject)
right <- seq_table |> filter(n > 13) |> rename(n_r = n, accept_r = accept, reject_r = reject)
bind_cols(left, right) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("n inspect", "n accept", "n reject", "n inspect", "n accept", "n reject"),
    align = "cccccc"
  )
```

So, for $n=24$ the acceptance number is 0 and the rejection number is 3. The "x" means that acceptance or rejection is not possible.

Other sequential plans are given below.

| n inspect | n accept | n reject |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 49  | 1 | 3 |
| 58  | 1 | 4 |
| 74  | 2 | 4 |
| 83  | 2 | 5 |
| 100 | 3 | 5 |
| 109 | 3 | 6 |

The corresponding single sampling plan is (52,2) and double sampling plan is (21,0), (21,1).

[**Efficiency measured by ASN**]{#sec-pmc-26-efficiency}

Efficiency for a sequential sampling scheme is measured by the *average sample number* ([ASN](#sec-pmc-22-asn)) required for a given [Type I](#sec-pmc-22-alpha) and [Type II](#sec-pmc-22-beta) set of errors. The number of samples needed when following a sequential sampling scheme may vary from trial to trial, and the ASN represents the average of what might happen over many trials with a fixed incoming defect level. Good software for designing sequential sampling schemes will calculate the ASN curve as a function of the incoming defect level.
